analysis.title: FAQs: Stuck in a 5% world
key_insights: BofA equity and quant strategy says bonds look more attractive than the S&P 500 than at any point in 20+ years on earnings yield and dividend yield. The 10yr Treasury yield is above the S&P 500 trailing earnings yield, the widest spread since the early 2000s.

Valuation is a poor near-term timing signal but a strong long-term predictor. Normalized P/E of 32x implies about -3% annualized S&P 500 returns over the next decade, versus about +3% for the equal-weighted index (normalized P/E 25x). With a 2% dividend yield the average stock is roughly a wash.
BofA still prefers stocks with positive gearing to nominal growth over both bonds and cash.

The team is encouraged that the Fed and Treasury Secretary focus on the long end of the curve. Aging demographics and possibly AI argue for disinflation and a lower rates ceiling than in the 1970s and 1980s.

Bond allocations are at multi-year lows: 48% of Global Fund Manager Survey investors are net underweight bonds, the biggest underweight since May 2022. Sell-side strategists recommend the lowest bond allocation since early 2022. Retirees hold $8tn in cash with an average CD yield of about 2%.

Rate thresholds for equities: 5% is where investors grew agnostic between bonds and stocks, 6% is where stock/bond correlation turns negative, and above 7% P/E multiples have compressed. The cause of rising rates matters: growth, productivity and deregulation are equity positive, while sovereign risk, buyers' strikes and inflation are not.

BofA rate strategists expect the 2yr and 10yr to end 2026 at 5%, and say 5.5%+ on the 10yr cannot be ruled out. BofA economists forecast two additional Fed hikes this year, and rate strategists see room for bear flattening.

The S&P 500 is more expensive ahead of its first hike than in any past tightening cycle except 1999-2000 (forward P/E 20.4 today). In three of the last eight hiking cycles the bull market peak fell within 6 months before to 12 months after the first hike.
Risk: if rates rise further because of higher inflation, multiples would likely keep contracting. The current P/E implies CPI of about 1.7%, far below BofA's inflation forecast.

Sectors most negatively sensitive to the 10yr over the last decade: Real Estate, Info Tech, Utilities, Comm Services and Discretionary. During bear flatteners Real Estate, Utilities and Financials lag most. Past hiking cycles hurt bond proxies, Comm Services, Discretionary and Financials; Tech, Staples, Energy and Health Care fared best.
Value factors outperformed most in the first 12 months of Fed hiking cycles and Risk factors lagged. For small caps, Value and Quality outperformed and Risk lagged.
Health Care has almost no rate sensitivity but has de-rated more than any other sector since hikes began, so it could hedge rate uncertainty.
Tech betas are less reliable: despite rising long rates, Semis and Tech Hardware have led this year. Big R&D spenders are hurt most by rising long rates, dividend growers helped most.

Banks analyst Ebrahim Poonawala says Fed hikes should modestly lift bank EPS because most banks are asset sensitive, but a sustained tightening could weigh on consumer and capital markets activity. Bear flatteners affect bank P/Es more than fundamentals.

Consumer: AMZN and TSLA are 61% of Discretionary. Household Durables (mostly homebuilders) could benefit if long rates peak. Residential real estate prices could reset lower as the gap between effective and quoted mortgage rates closes, and wealth gains have not predicted future stock returns.

Corporate leverage is better than in prior cycles: S&P 500 net debt/EBITDA is below average, effective cost of debt is below 4%, and about 80% of debt is long-term fixed, up from about 58% in 2007. The annualized EPS hit from higher interest expense in 2026-2028 is under 1%, largest in REITs and Telecom.

Small caps carry more risk: over 40% of Russell 2000 ex-Financials debt is short-term or floating, with a large share maturing in the next several years. Government net interest expense as a share of GDP is at a record high.

BofA argues against selling the S&P 500 on rate volatility: the probability of loss falls from 46% over a day to 5% over a decade. Missing the 10 best days per decade cut returns to 140% versus 35,000% for staying invested. The S&P 500 typically has three 5% pullbacks and one 10% correction a year; only one 5% pullback (March) has occurred this year.

earnings_insights: BofA estimates the annualized EPS hit to the S&P 500 ex-Financials from higher interest expense in 2026-2028 is under 1%, assuming three Fed hikes in 2026 and then a pause. The largest hits are in REITs and Telecom and the smallest in Semis and Media & Entertainment.
Banks analyst Ebrahim Poonawala expects Fed hikes to be a modest boost to bank EPS because most banks are asset sensitive.

tension_points.bull_case: Bonds look cheap against stocks on earnings and dividend yield, demographics and policy focus on the long end support a lower rates ceiling, and bond allocations are at multi-year lows.
tension_points.bear_case: The S&P 500 is expensive ahead of Fed hikes (forward P/E 20.4, highest ahead of tightening since 1999), and BofA still prefers stocks with positive gearing to nominal growth over bonds and cash.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Rates rising because of higher inflation rather than growth, which would keep compressing multiples, or the 10yr moving above 7%, where P/E multiples have compressed.

theme_stances.key_argument: Bonds are more attractive relative to the S&P 500 than at any point in the past 20+ years based on earnings and dividend yield.

theme_stances.key_argument: Real Estate, Info Tech, Utilities and Comm Services have the most negative betas to the 10yr, and bear flatteners hurt Real Estate, Utilities and Financials.
theme_stances.evidence: Real Estate, Utilities, and Financials have been the biggest laggards

theme_stances.key_argument: Extending the time horizon has been one of the most effective ways to avoid losses, and panic selling is costly.
theme_stances.evidence: Panic selling can be costly given that the best days often follow the worst days.
